decks.domain: Vehicle registration, title, insurance, inspection and efficient driving

cards.front: What does the maintenance of financial responsibility law require?
cards.back: Vermont's maintenance of financial responsibility law requires the vehicle you drive to be covered by liability insurance, and liability and property damage coverage protect you from financial loss when bodily injury or property damage occurs.

cards.front: What are the minimum liability insurance amounts?
cards.back: Coverage must be at least twenty-five thousand dollars for death or injury of one person, fifty thousand dollars for death or injury of two or more persons and ten thousand dollars for property damage.

cards.front: What do the three minimum insurance amounts each cover?
cards.back: Twenty-five thousand dollars covers one person's death or injury, fifty thousand covers two or more people, and ten thousand covers property damage.

cards.front: When must the insurance card be shown?
cards.back: You must carry an insurance card from your insurer in the vehicle showing the vehicle is covered, and must show it when stopped by a police officer and when taking a driving test.

cards.front: What happens if you are stopped without insurance, and if you have insurance but no card?
cards.back: A driver stopped without insurance receives a ticket, a fine and two points on the driving record, while an insured driver who cannot show the card at the stop has fifteen days to produce a card proving coverage at the time of the stop.

cards.front: How does being uninsured at a stop differ from lacking the card?
cards.back: Being uninsured at a stop earns a ticket, fine and two points, whereas being insured but cardless earns fifteen days to produce the card.

cards.front: When does driving without insurance cost you the license, and for how long must proof be shown?
cards.back: Driving without insurance and then having a crash even if not at fault, driving under the influence, taking a vehicle without consent, driving while suspended, revoked or refused, causing a death or leaving a crash scene costs you the license until you get insurance, with proof required for a full three years.
cards.memory_hook: Losing the license for no insurance

decks.domain: Vehicle registration, title, insurance, inspection and efficient driving

cards.front: Who must register a vehicle, and how soon must a new resident do it?
cards.back: A Vermont resident must register any vehicle driven on the roads, and a person moving in from another state must register the vehicle within sixty days of moving into Vermont.

cards.front: What are the deadlines for registering as a new resident, mailing trade paperwork and reporting a change?
cards.back: A new resident has sixty days to register a vehicle, while a sale paperwork package after a trade must be mailed within twenty-four hours and a name, address or color change must be reported within thirty days.
cards.memory_hook: Sixty days, twenty-four hours, thirty days

cards.front: Where must proof of registration be kept, and who may see it?
cards.back: Proof of valid registration must always be in the vehicle while it is in use and a police officer has the right to see it.

cards.front: How must registration plates be attached, kept and lit?
cards.back: Registration plates must be firmly attached so they cannot loosen, no part may be covered or hidden, they must be kept clean, and the rear plate must be lit so it can be read from at least fifty feet away.

cards.front: May plates be used on another vehicle, and when may they transfer?
cards.back: The number plates issued for a vehicle may be used only on that vehicle, but you may transfer them to a new vehicle you buy when you trade in or sell the old one.

cards.front: How soon must a name, address or vehicle color change be reported?
cards.back: A change of your name, your address or the color of your vehicle must be reported to the DMV within thirty days.
cards.memory_hook: Reporting name, address or color changes

decks.domain: Vehicle registration, title, insurance, inspection and efficient driving

cards.front: What must a seller provide and do when selling a vehicle?
cards.back: When selling a vehicle give the buyer a bill of sale with the buyer's name, the seller's signature, the date, and the vehicle's year, make, serial number and sale price, sign the back of the title with the new owner's name and address, the mileage and the date, and remove your plates.

cards.front: When is a signed odometer statement required?
cards.back: An odometer statement signed by both seller and buyer is required on every sale of a vehicle of model year twenty eleven or newer, and the statement is part of the title or the Vermont bill of sale.

cards.front: What steps and deadline apply when trading vehicles?
cards.back: When trading vehicles exchange bills of sale, have the title to the vehicle you receive signed over to you, remove your plates from the old vehicle and put them on the new one if you transfer the registration, and mail the registration, tax and title application with the title and fees to the DMV in Montpelier within twenty-four hours.

cards.front: How can a lost registration certificate be replaced?
cards.back: A lost registration certificate can be replaced at any DMV office, by mail or online.

decks.module: Purchase and use tax and titles
decks.domain: Vehicle registration, title, insurance, inspection and efficient driving

cards.front: Where is a replacement plate application available?
cards.back: If one or both registration plates are lost, a Replacement Plate Application is available at any DMV office, at a police station or online.

cards.front: How is the purchase and use tax calculated on a non leased vehicle?
cards.back: Buying a new or used non leased vehicle triggers the purchase and use tax of six percent of the price paid or the current fair market value, whichever is greater.

cards.front: How does the tax base differ between a purchase and a lease?
cards.back: The purchase and use tax is six percent of the higher of price or fair market value for a purchase, but six percent of acquisition cost minus lease end value for a lease.

cards.front: When is a new resident exempt from the purchase and use tax?
cards.back: A new resident registering a vehicle acquired outside Vermont on which they or their spouse already paid a sales or use tax is exempt from the Vermont tax when the tax paid elsewhere equals or exceeds Vermont's, or when the vehicle was registered for at least three years in a jurisdiction that collects such a tax, and otherwise owes the difference.

cards.front: What paperwork must accompany a leased vehicle registration, and what if it is missing?
cards.back: A leased vehicle from a Vermont dealer must be registered with a purchase and use tax computation form or the lease agreement or dealer worksheet, and without them the vehicle is taxed at six percent of the acquisition cost.

cards.front: How is the taxable cost of a leased vehicle calculated?
cards.back: The taxable cost of a leased vehicle is six percent of the acquisition cost minus the lease end value as stated in the computation form, lease agreement or dealer worksheet, regardless of whether there is an option to buy at lease end.

cards.front: Which vehicles need a Vermont title, and which are excepted?
cards.back: Every vehicle must have a Vermont motor vehicle title, with exceptions such as a motorcycle under three hundred cubic centimeters of engine displacement and a trailer with an empty weight of fifteen hundred pounds or less.

cards.front: What documents are needed to register a new or used vehicle?
cards.back: A Manufacturer's Certificate of Origin is required for every new vehicle and no new vehicle can be registered without it, and any vehicle registered in Vermont needs a registration application, the bill of sale and the former owner's title signed over.

decks.module: Identification numbers, rebuilt titles and liens
decks.domain: Vehicle registration, title, insurance, inspection and efficient driving

cards.front: What is a vehicle identification number, and how long has it been seventeen characters?
cards.back: A vehicle identification number is a unique seventeen character code of digits and capital letters that identifies a specific vehicle and its features, specifications and manufacturer, and before nineteen eighty-one such numbers varied from eleven to seventeen characters.
cards.memory_hook: What a vehicle identification number is

cards.front: What is the identification number, and when must it be verified?
cards.back: A seventeen character identification number is standard since nineteen eighty-one, and verification of it is required only for salvage, bonded title and foreign registered vehicles.

cards.front: Which vehicles need identification number verification, and who performs it?
cards.back: Vehicle identification number verification is required for vehicles with salvage documentation, vehicles being titled under bond and vehicles registered in any foreign country including Canada, and it must be done in Vermont by a law enforcement officer, supervised law enforcement personnel or a designated DMV employee.

cards.front: What title does a salvage vehicle receive, and what check is required?
cards.back: A vehicle registered in Vermont with a salvage title receives a title marked rebuilt vehicle, and registering it requires having the identification number checked by a DMV employee or Vermont law enforcement with the verification section of the application completed.

cards.front: What is a lien, and who holds the title until the loan is repaid?
cards.back: Borrowing money from a bank, credit union or another person to buy a vehicle puts a lien on it, the lender is the lien holder whose name must be on the registration application, and the title is sent to the lien holder and withheld from you until the loan is repaid.

decks.domain: Vehicle registration, title, insurance, inspection and efficient driving

cards.front: How often must a vehicle be inspected, and when after registration?
cards.back: A vehicle must be inspected once a year and kept running properly at all times, a badly running vehicle can put you at fault in a crash, the sticker shows when the next inspection is due, and a newly registered vehicle must be inspected within fifteen days unless it already bears a valid Vermont sticker.

cards.front: How soon must a newly registered vehicle be inspected, and how often after that?
cards.back: A newly registered vehicle must be inspected within fifteen days, while every vehicle is then inspected once a year as the sticker shows.

cards.front: What does the handbook say about interstate speed and fuel economy?
cards.back: Driving fifty-five or sixty miles per hour on the interstate instead of sixty-five saves fuel, and the Environmental Protection Agency estimates up to a fifteen percent improvement in fuel economy from that tip alone.

cards.front: How do smooth acceleration and braking save fuel?
cards.back: Accelerating smoothly from a stop and braking softly saves fuel, while fast starts, weaving and hard braking waste fuel and wear brakes and tires faster, so keep a safe distance and anticipate traffic to brake and accelerate gradually.

cards.front: Why avoid idling, and how long should warm ups and idling last?
cards.back: Idling wastes fuel, wears the engine and can cause respiratory illness, so clear snow and ice before starting, limit stationary warm ups to about thirty seconds when possible, and in town idling more than ten seconds uses more fuel than shutting off and restarting.

cards.front: What does Vermont's unattended motor vehicle law require?
cards.back: Leaving a vehicle idling unattended in public violates Vermont's unattended motor vehicle law, so if you leave the vehicle you must shut it off.

cards.front: How does tire pressure affect fuel use and tire wear?
cards.back: Keeping tires at the recommended pressure shown on the driver's door jamb placard and in the owner's manual can cut average fuel use by three to four percent, while under inflated tires raise rolling resistance, lower fuel economy and wear faster.

cards.front: How do maintenance and extra weight affect fuel use?
cards.back: Keep the engine tuned, the wheels aligned and the air filters replaced as recommended, and carry no unnecessary weight such as trunk clutter or heavy roof luggage, because misaligned wheels and extra weight make the engine work harder and burn more fuel.

cards.front: How does air conditioner use affect fuel, and what alternatives help?
cards.back: Use heating and air conditioning selectively, since cutting air conditioner use when temperatures exceed eighty degrees can save ten to fifteen percent of fuel, prefer the vent setting and park in the shade.

cards.front: How do open windows, trip planning and car pooling affect fuel use?
cards.back: Drive with the windows closed unless your speed stays under fifty miles per hour, because open windows at highway speed add aerodynamic drag and lower fuel economy, and consolidate trips and car pool to save miles and fuel.
